# Shoulder dislocation

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Shoulder dislocation*

[Original Article Link](/library/P30Wif)

---

## Summary

In shoulder <u>dislocation</u>, the <u>head of the humerus</u> dislocates completely or partially (subluxation) in one of three directions: <u>anterior</u> (most common), <u>posterior</u>, or inferior. Shoulder <u>dislocation</u> is usually the result of trauma, and, because the <u>head of the humerus</u> is substantially larger than the <u>glenoid fossa</u>, it is the most common type of <u>joint</u> <u>dislocation</u>. Typical symptoms include <u>pain</u> and restricted <u>range of motion</u>. Examination reveals a palpable dent in the shoulder caused by the empty <u>glenoid fossa</u>, while the <u>head of the humerus</u> may be palpable <u>anterior</u> or inferior to the <u>glenoid fossa</u>. <u>X-rays</u> of the shoulder in at least two views are necessary to rule out <u>fractures</u> and confirm the diagnosis. With adequate <u>analgesia</u> and muscle relaxation, the <u>head of the humerus</u> can be carefully repositioned into the <u>glenoid fossa</u> through various maneuvers. Reduction is followed by <u>immobilization</u> and subsequent <u>rehabilitation</u>. Patients with concomitant <u>soft tissue</u> lesions or recurrent shoulder <u>dislocation</u> may require <u>surgery</u> to stabilize the <u>shoulder joint</u>. Possible <u>complications of shoulder dislocation</u> include neurovascular damage (most commonly <u>axillary nerve injury</u>), continued instability, restricted <u>range of motion</u>, and <u>rotator cuff injury</u>.




For details on <u>closed reduction</u> techniques for <u>anterior</u> shoulder <u>dislocations</u>, see “<u>Shoulder reduction</u>.”

---

## Epidemiology

* Most common <u>joint</u> <u>dislocation</u>

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[1]](/library/rh0f2f)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–29 years of age [[1]](/library/rh0f2f)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Anatomy: The <u>head of the humerus</u> is larger than the shallow <u>glenoid fossa</u>, which accounts for the high <u>incidence</u> of shoulder <u>dislocation</u>.

* Trauma (e.g., falling on an outstretched arm): commonly associated with contact sports [[1]](/library/rh0f2f)

* Predisposing factors for recurrent shoulder <u>dislocation</u>

* <u>Rotator cuff tear</u>

* Damage to the <u>glenohumeral ligament</u>

* <u>Bankart lesion</u> and <u>Hill-Sachs lesion</u>

* Loose <u>joint capsule</u>

* For <u>posterior</u> <u>dislocation</u>: uncoordinated muscle contraction (e.g., <u>seizure</u>, <u>electrical shock</u>)

---

## Classification

* Anterior shoulder dislocation: displacement of the <u>humeral head</u> <u>anterior</u> (and often also inferior) to the glenohumeral fossa (> 95% of cases) [[2]](/library/5wXijZ0)[[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)

* Posterior shoulder dislocation: displacement of the <u>humeral head</u> <u>posterior</u> to the glenohumeral fossa (< 4% of cases) [[4]](/library/J_Ws6L0)

* Inferior shoulder dislocation: displacement of the <u>humeral head</u> inferior to the glenohumeral fossa (< 1% of cases)  [[5]](/library/q_WC6L0)





![Inferior shoulder dislocation (luxatio erecta) after a fall from a ladder](media/in1v3q2v6wx8xrkya0617pm4.jpg)

Inferior shoulder dislocation (luxatio erecta) after a fall from a ladder

---

## Clinical features

* General symptoms

* Severe shoulder <u>pain</u>

* Resistance to shoulder and arm movement

* Empty <u>glenoid fossa</u>: A palpable or visible dent may be present where the <u>humeral head</u> is expected.

* <u>Anterior shoulder dislocation</u> [[2]](/library/5wXijZ0)[[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)  

* Arm typically held in <u>abduction</u> and slight <u>external rotation</u> (limited <u>adduction</u>)

* <u>Humeral head</u> palpable below the <u>coracoid process</u>

* Loss of shoulder contour: prominent <u>acromion</u> and flattening of the <u>deltoid muscle</u>

* <u>Posterior shoulder dislocation</u> [[4]](/library/J_Ws6L0)

* Arm held in <u>adduction</u> and <u>internal rotation</u> (limited <u>external rotation</u>)

* Prominent <u>coracoid process</u> with <u>anterior</u> <u>soft tissue</u> flattening

* <u>Humeral head</u> not palpable [[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)

* <u>Inferior shoulder dislocation</u> [[5]](/library/q_WC6L0)

* Arm held in fixed <u>abduction</u> at ∼ 125° (limited <u>adduction</u>)

* <u>Humeral head</u> may be palpable in <u>axilla</u>

* <u>Elbow</u> typically held in <u>flexion</u> with a <u>pronated</u> forearm

* <u>Axillary nerve injury</u> may be present.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Posterior shoulder dislocation</u> is frequently overlooked during <u>clinical examination</u>. [[7]](/library/I_WYpL0)

## Diagnosis

### Clinical evaluation [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)[[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)




Signs of <u>neurovascular injury</u> or <u>fracture-dislocation</u> on <u>clinical examination</u> should prompt urgent orthopedic consultation.




* Assess for <u>signs of a fracture</u> (e.g., concomitant <u>humerus fracture</u>).

* Conduct a <u>neurovascular examination</u> to identify: [[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)

* <u>Axillary nerve palsy</u>

* <u>Brachial plexus injury</u>

* <u>Radial nerve palsy</u>

* <u>Median nerve palsy</u>

* <u>Ulnar nerve palsy</u>

* Recurrent uncomplicated <u>anterior shoulder dislocation</u> can be <u>diagnosed clinically</u>.  [[8]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





> [!WARNING]
> The risk of concomitant <u>fracture</u> is increased in patients with age > 40 years, first-time <u>dislocation</u>, or a severe injury mechanism (e.g., <u>MVC</u>, fall > 1 flight of stairs, or interpersonal violence). [[9]](/library/YzWnrL0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Axillary nerve injury</u> is common with <u>inferior shoulder dislocation</u>. Document signs of <u>axillary nerve palsy</u> prior to manipulation and reduce without delay (see “Treatment”). [[5]](/library/q_WC6L0)




### Shoulder x‑ray




* Goal: confirm <u>dislocation</u> and exclude <u>fracture</u>

* Views [[10]](/library/t_WXJL0)[[11]](/library/y_WdIL0)

* Anteroposterior view (AP view) with the shoulder in internal and <u>external rotation</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> scapular view (Y view): a radiographic angle where the body of the <u>scapula</u> forms the letter "Y" with the <u>coracoid process</u> and the <u>acromion</u>     [[11]](/library/y_WdIL0)

* Axillary view: a radiographic angle visualizing the <u>glenohumeral joint</u> axially from the inferior aspect with the arm in <u>abduction</u>  [[11]](/library/y_WdIL0)

* Findings

* Displacement of the <u>humeral head</u> from the <u>glenoid fossa</u> [[11]](/library/y_WdIL0)

* <u>Anterior shoulder dislocation</u>: <u>humeral head</u> may be overlapping with and/or inferior to the glenoid on the AP view; <u>anterior</u> displacement visible on the <u>Y view</u> and axillary view

* <u>Posterior shoulder dislocation</u>: displacement may not be visible on AP view; <u>posterior</u> displacement visible on the <u>Y view</u> and axillary view

* <u>Inferior shoulder dislocation</u>: <u>humeral head</u> inferior to the glenoid on the AP view and <u>humerus</u> <u>abducted</u>; inferior displacement visible on <u>Y view</u> [[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)

* <u>Radiographic fracture signs</u> may be present if there is a concomitant <u>fracture</u>.

* Light bulb sign: diagnostic of <u>posterior shoulder dislocation</u> on the AP view    [[8]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Hill-Sachs lesion</u> and/or <u>Bankart lesion</u> may be visible.





> [!WARNING]
> Obtain a <u>Y view</u> and/or axillary view in addition to the AP view to reduce the risk of missing or misclassifying shoulder <u>dislocations</u> (especially <u>posterior shoulder dislocation</u>). [[10]](/library/t_WXJL0)[[11]](/library/y_WdIL0)

### <u>MRI</u> [[10]](/library/t_WXJL0)




* Goal: deeper evaluation of <u>soft tissue</u> injuries related to <u>dislocation</u> event

* Indications

* <u>Hill-Sachs lesion</u> or <u>Bankart lesion</u> identified on <u>x-ray</u>

* Normal <u>x-ray</u> despite history consistent with <u>dislocation</u> event

* Modalities: <u>MRI</u> shoulder without IV contrast or <u>MR arthrography</u>

## Treatment

The primary aim of treatment is to <u>reposition</u> the <u>humeral head</u> into the <u>glenoid cavity</u> and restore full <u>range of motion</u>.




### Initial management [[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)




* Patients with <u>polytrauma</u>: Follow the <u>ABCDE approach</u>.

* Patients with <u>posterior shoulder dislocation</u>: <u>Treat acute seizures</u> or <u>manage electrical injuries</u>, if present.

* All patients: <u>Manage acute pain</u> and consider a broad <u>arm sling</u> to immobilize in a position of comfort while waiting for imaging.

* If indicated, initiate steps for immediate <u>closed reduction</u>, e.g., <u>preparation for procedural sedation</u>.

* Consult orthopedics if reduction by a specialist or <u>surgery</u> is required.





![Broad arm sling using triangular bandage](media/gx1gycx4tur8z97u5ss2jlqh.jpg)

Broad arm sling using triangular bandage




### <u>Closed reduction</u> [[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)




#### Indications




* Consider urgent <u>closed reduction</u> for all uncomplicated shoulder <u>dislocations</u>. [[12]](/library/cx1avQ0)

* See “<u>Indications for shoulder reduction</u>” for reasons to consult orthopedics before attempting reduction.





#### Techniques




* <u>Anterior shoulder dislocation</u>

* Multiple recommended techniques exist with similar success and complication rates.  [[12]](/library/cx1avQ0)[[13]](/library/ttWX2M0)[[14]](/library/UzWbHL0)[[15]](/library/3wYSir)

* See “<u>Shoulder reduction</u>” for details on, e.g., <u>scapular manipulation</u>, <u>Milch technique</u>, and <u>traction-countertraction</u>.

* <u>Procedural sedation</u> is often required.

* <u>Posterior shoulder dislocation</u>: typically reduced under <u>general anesthesia</u>  [[4]](/library/J_Ws6L0)

* <u>Inferior shoulder dislocation</u> [[5]](/library/q_WC6L0)

* Consider <u>traction-countertraction</u> OR gentle rotation of the <u>humeral head</u> to convert it to an <u>anterior</u> <u>dislocation</u>, followed by an <u>anterior</u> <u>dislocation</u> reduction technique.

* Consult orthopedics if the <u>humeral head</u> is entrapped, e.g., by the <u>glenohumeral ligament</u> or <u>joint capsule</u>.





#### Post-reduction care [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)




* Repeat <u>neurovascular examination</u> and imaging to evaluate reduction success and identify complications (e.g., <u>Hill-Sachs lesion</u>).

* Apply an <u>arm sling</u> or <u>shoulder immobilizer</u>.      [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)[[16]](/library/K_WU6L0)[[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)[[17]](/library/hzWcsL0)[[18]](/library/3zWSsL0)

* Provide <u>analgesia</u>, e.g., <u>acetaminophen</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, and/or ice packs.

* Ensure short-term follow-up (e.g., in 5–8 days) for orthopedics assessment and subsequent <u>rehabilitation</u>.

* Counsel patients on the risk of early recurrence and advise avoidance of contact sports until fully healed.  [[16]](/library/K_WU6L0)





> [!WARNING]
> Conduct a thorough <u>neurovascular examination</u> before and after <u>shoulder reduction</u> to identify <u>axillary nerve injury</u> and other <u>neurovascular injuries</u> as early as possible. [[6]](/library/ezWx7L0)

### Surgical management




Surgical management may be indicated for complicated shoulder <u>dislocation</u> or for prevention and treatment of recurrent shoulder <u>dislocations</u>.




#### Complicated shoulder <u>dislocation</u> [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)




* Examples

* <u>Fracture-dislocation</u> (e.g., concomitant <u>proximal humerus fracture</u>, <u>clavicle fracture</u>, or <u>scapula</u> <u>fracture</u>)

* <u>Open dislocation</u>

* Unsuccessful <u>closed reduction</u>

* <u>Neurovascular injury</u>

* Associated <u>rotator cuff tear</u> (more common in patients > 40 years of age)

* Management

* Urgent operative intervention (e.g., <u>ORIF</u>) may be required, e.g., for displaced <u>fracture-dislocations</u> and other associated injuries.

* Most otherwise uncomplicated irreducible shoulder <u>dislocations</u> are treated with <u>closed reduction</u> under <u>general anesthesia</u>. [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)





#### Recurrent shoulder <u>dislocation</u> [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)[[16]](/library/K_WU6L0)




* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Demographic factors: age < 30 years, active lifestyle, male sex [[16]](/library/K_WU6L0)

* Glenohumeral instability, e.g., caused by <u>Bankart lesions</u>, <u>Hill-Sachs</u> lesions, <u>glenoid labrum injury</u>, glenoid rim <u>fracture</u> (bony Bankart lesion)

* Management: Elective operative intervention is often recommended (e.g., <u>arthroscopic</u> <u>surgery</u>, open <u>surgery</u>).





> [!TIP]
> Young, active patients with first-time uncomplicated shoulder <u>dislocations</u> are likely to benefit from <u>surgery</u> and should be referred to orthopedics after successful <u>closed reduction</u>. [[3]](/library/p_WL6L0)

---

## Complications

* <u>Neurovascular injury</u>: can be a complication of both <u>dislocation</u> and reduction

* <u>Axillary nerve injury</u>

* <u>Brachial plexus injury</u>

* Injury of the <u>axillary artery</u> and/or <u>axillary vein</u>

* Hill-Sachs lesion ;   [[19]](/library/Fadgmo0)

* A <u>depression</u> <u>fracture</u> on the posterolateral surface of the <u>humeral head</u> caused by impact with the glenoid rim

* Highly prevalent in patients with an <u>anterior shoulder dislocation</u>

* Increases the risk of glenohumeral instability and recurrent shoulder <u>dislocation</u>

* <u>Bankart lesion</u>

* <u>Avulsion fracture</u> of the major and/or minor tubercles

* <u>Shoulder joint</u> instability

* <u>Rotator cuff injury</u>

* Shoulder stiffness  due to prolonged <u>immobilization</u>

* <u>Osteoarthritis</u> of the <u>shoulder joint</u>





> [!TIP]
> A sensory deficit over the <u>lateral</u> surface of the shoulder and limited <u>abduction</u> due to <u>deltoid muscle</u> <u>weakness</u> suggest <u>axillary nerve injury</u>. [[8]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




![Anterior shoulder dislocation with Hill-Sachs lesion](media/g8stdfi0sh4pt787vggaogrn.jpg)

Anterior shoulder dislocation with Hill-Sachs lesion




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
